title: Heat transfer: conduction, convection and radiation
voiceInstructions: Warm, engaging female teacher with a natural General American English accent. Relaxed, welcoming and lightly playful, with a gentle smile and conversational rhythm. Keep scientific terms precise and avoid an announcer cadence. Slow down for equations, numbers and conversions. Give brief natural thinking pauses after questions. Do not add words or laughter absent from the script.

sources.title: NTA: Official JEE Main 2026 syllabus, Physics Unit 7

chapters.title: Three routes for energy transfer
chapters.formula: Conduction: microscopic exchange; convection: fluid motion; radiation: electromagnetic waves
points: Conduction does not require bulk transport of the material.
Convection transports energy through fluid motion.
Radiation can carry energy through a vacuum.
chapters.script: Hey, welcome back. Touch the handle of a metal spoon left in hot soup, watch the soup circulate, and feel warmth from a nearby heater without touching it. Those experiences point to three different ways energy travels. Conduction transfers energy through microscopic interactions without a bulk flow of the material. In metals, mobile electrons also help carry energy. Convection involves fluid moving from place to place and carrying internal energy with it. Warm fluid often rises because it becomes less dense in a gravitational field, but a fan or pump can also drive forced convection. Radiation carries energy as electromagnetic waves and does not need any material between source and receiver. That's how sunlight reaches Earth through space. Real situations often involve all three mechanisms. A hot cooking vessel conducts through its wall, circulates liquid by convection, and radiates to its surroundings. So don't force every situation into just one category unless the question asks which mechanism dominates. We will calculate steady conduction and thermal radiation, then use a simple cooling model. Keep the distinction between heat and its rate of transfer clear. Heat is measured in joules; transfer rate is energy per second, measured in watts.

chapters.title: Steady conduction through a slab
chapters.formula: H = k A (Thot - Tcold)/L; H = Q/t
points: k is thermal conductivity in W/(m K).
For fixed boundary temperatures, a thicker slab conducts less power.
k = 0.5 W/(m K), A = 2 m squared, L = 0.1 m and Delta T = 20 K give H = 200 W.
chapters.script: Imagine a flat slab with one face held warm and the other held cooler. After the temperature profile settles, energy crosses the slab at a steady rate. For uniform material, no internal generation and negligible side losses, that rate equals thermal conductivity times area times temperature difference, divided by thickness. Conductivity tells us how readily the material conducts. A larger face offers more parallel paths for transfer. Greater thickness makes the transfer path longer. Let's use conductivity zero point five watts per metre per kelvin, face area two square metres, thickness zero point one metres, and temperature difference twenty kelvin. Multiply zero point five by two by twenty, then divide by zero point one. The rate is two hundred watts. Over sixty seconds, it transfers twelve thousand joules if the boundary temperatures stay fixed. Pause and predict what doubling the thickness does. It halves the rate, not the energy per degree stored inside the material. Conductivity and specific heat are different properties. The minus sign in the differential conduction law describes flow toward lower temperature; here we are calculating the positive magnitude. Steady state does not mean both slab faces have the same temperature. It means the temperature at each location stops changing with time while energy continues to flow.

chapters.title: Two layers: thermal resistance
chapters.formula: R = L/(k A); H = Delta T/(R1 + R2)
points: Steady series layers carry the same power.
Temperature drops are H R for each layer.
Resistances 0.2 and 0.3 K/W across 50 K give 100 W and drops of 20 and 30 K.
chapters.script: Now stack two insulating layers, so energy must pass through the first and then the second. We can make the algebra friendlier by defining thermal resistance: thickness divided by conductivity times area. Its unit is kelvin per watt. A large resistance needs a large temperature difference to pass a given power. In steady series conduction, both layers carry the same transfer rate, otherwise energy would keep accumulating at their interface. Add their resistances. If the two resistances are zero point two and zero point three kelvin per watt, and the outer faces differ by fifty kelvin, divide fifty by zero point five. The rate is one hundred watts. How much temperature drop belongs to each layer? Multiply the common rate by each resistance. The drops are twenty kelvin and thirty kelvin. If the hot face is eighty degrees Celsius and the cold face thirty, the interface is sixty degrees Celsius. Notice that the greater resistance takes the greater temperature drop. We assume perfect contact and no side losses; an imperfect contact can introduce an extra resistance. For separate side by side paths with the same boundary temperatures, add the transfer rates instead of adding series resistances. First sketch the path energy must follow. That simple sketch tells you whether the layers are in series or in parallel.

chapters.title: Radiation requires absolute temperature
points: Use kelvin in fourth-power radiation expressions.
A blackbody has emissivity 1; ideal emissivity lies between 0 and 1.
With epsilon = 1, A = 0.1 m squared, sigma = 5.67 x 10^-8, T = 400 K and surroundings 300 K, net power is 99.225 W.
chapters.script: Unlike conduction, thermal radiation can cross a vacuum. For a body facing a large surrounding enclosure, our simple net radiation model uses emissivity times the Stefan Boltzmann constant times area times the difference of fourth powers of absolute temperatures. The body emits radiation, and it also absorbs radiation from its surroundings. Net loss means we subtract the incoming contribution. Take an ideal blackbody of area zero point one square metres, at four hundred kelvin, surrounded by a large enclosure at three hundred kelvin. Use sigma five point six seven times ten to the power minus eight. The difference of the fourth powers is seventeen point five times ten to the power nine. Multiplying gives net power ninety nine point two two five watts. Don't put Celsius temperatures into a fourth power formula, and don't subtract the temperatures before raising to the fourth power. Doubling absolute temperature makes the emitted power sixteen times larger if area and emissivity stay fixed. But net power is not generally multiplied by sixteen, because the surrounding temperature term remains. A blackbody has emissivity one. Real emissivity depends on surface and wavelength; we are using a simple effective value. Shiny and dark surfaces can behave differently, but colour alone is not a universal rule for infrared emissivity.

chapters.title: Newton's cooling law and a comparison problem
chapters.formula: dT/dt = -b (T - Ts); excess temperature decays exponentially for constant b
points: Newton's cooling law is an approximation under suitable conditions.
For the same body and unchanged conditions, initial cooling rate scales with temperature excess.
At surroundings 20 C, a body at 60 C initially cools twice as fast as the same body at 40 C.
chapters.script: Let's finish with Newton's law of cooling. In a useful approximate model, the cooling rate is proportional to how much warmer the body is than its surroundings. The rate of change of temperature is minus a constant times the temperature excess. We assume nearly uniform body temperature and conditions that keep this constant approximately fixed. Suppose the room is twenty degrees Celsius. Compare the same body initially at sixty degrees with that body initially at forty degrees. The excess temperatures are forty and twenty degrees. So the first initial cooling rate has twice the magnitude. The comparison uses temperature differences, so Celsius is fine here. It does not mean the body loses the same number of degrees each minute. As it cools, the excess becomes smaller and the cooling slows. For a constant model coefficient, temperature excess decays exponentially. After one interval halves the excess, a second equal interval halves what remains, not the original temperature. A body starting at sixty in a twenty degree room would then reach forty, then thirty, under that example. Newton's law is not an exact substitute for the fourth power radiation law at arbitrary temperatures. For a small difference near a fixed surrounding temperature, radiation can approximately contribute a term proportional to the difference. Identify the mechanism, the assumptions and the units before choosing your equation. That's your heat transfer toolkit.

quiz.question: Which mechanism can transfer energy across a vacuum?
quiz.explanation: Electromagnetic radiation needs no material medium; conduction and convection rely on matter.

quiz.question: A slab has k = 0.5 W/(m K), A = 2 m squared, L = 0.1 m, and face temperature difference 20 K. Steady heat-transfer rate is:
quiz.explanation: H = k A Delta T/L = 0.5 x 2 x 20/0.1 = 200 W.

quiz.question: Series thermal resistances 0.2 and 0.3 K/W connect outer faces at 80 and 30 C. Interface temperature is:
quiz.explanation: H = 50/0.5 = 100 W. The first layer drops 100 x 0.2 = 20 K, so the interface is 80 - 20 = 60 C.
